hook.text: You chose to read this. That choice had alternatives, costs, and consequences—even if you didn't notice them.

buildup.text: A decision is selecting one option from a set of alternatives, each with different possible outcomes.

discovery.text: Decision theory studies how rational agents should choose—and how real humans actually do.

twist.text: Not deciding is also a decision. Delay, avoidance, and inaction all carry their own consequences.

climax.text: Every decision has three parts: options available, outcomes possible, and how much you value each outcome.

punchline.text: Choose or the world chooses for you.

quiz.question: What are the three parts of every decision?

hook.text: Economists assumed humans always maximize self-interest. Then researchers watched real people—and found chaos.

buildup.text: Rational choice theory says people pick the option that gives them the highest expected benefit.

discovery.text: It's an idealization—a benchmark for how a perfectly logical agent would behave.

twist.text: Real humans use shortcuts, follow emotions, and often prefer a sure small gain over a risky larger one.

climax.text: The theory isn't wrong—it's incomplete. It describes what we should do, not always what we actually do.

punchline.text: The rational ideal is a compass, not a portrait.

quiz.question: What does rational choice theory assume?
options: People select options that maximize expected benefit

hook.text: You tried on 40 pairs of jeans to find the perfect fit. Your friend grabbed the first good pair and left happy.

buildup.text: Maximizers search for the best possible option. Satisficers pick the first option that meets their threshold.

discovery.text: Herbert Simon coined satisficing—a blend of satisfy and suffice. It's how bounded rationality actually works.

twist.text: Research shows maximizers often get objectively better outcomes but feel worse about them. More choice, more regret.

climax.text: When stakes are low, satisfice. When stakes are high, maximize—but set a stopping rule first.

punchline.text: Good enough is often the best choice.

quiz.question: What is satisficing?
options: Choosing the first option that meets a minimum threshold

hook.text: You spent Saturday studying. The opportunity cost wasn't money—it was the hike, the nap, and the party you missed.

buildup.text: Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative you gave up when you chose something else.

discovery.text: Every choice silently kills other possibilities. Ignoring this leads to hidden overspending of time and resources.

twist.text: Thinking in opportunity costs is uncomfortable—it forces you to see what you sacrifice, not just what you gain.

climax.text: Before any commitment, ask: what's the best thing I could do instead? That's your real price.

punchline.text: Every yes is a hidden no.

quiz.question: What is opportunity cost?
options: The value of the best alternative given up
The total cost of all options

hook.text: Jeff Bezos splits decisions into two types: one-way doors you can't walk back through, and two-way doors you can.

buildup.text: Reversible decisions can be undone cheaply. Irreversible ones lock you into consequences permanently.

discovery.text: Most decisions are reversible—but we treat them as permanent, causing paralysis over trivial choices.

twist.text: Truly irreversible decisions—marriage, surgery, quitting—deserve careful analysis. Lunch orders don't.

climax.text: Match your decision effort to the decision's reversibility. Big locks need big keys.

punchline.text: Two-way door? Walk through fast.

quiz.question: Why does reversibility matter in decision-making?
options: All decisions should be treated equally
Irreversible decisions deserve more careful analysis

hook.text: A coin flip: heads you win $200, tails you lose $100. Should you play? Your gut says risky. Math says absolutely.

buildup.text: Expected value multiplies each outcome by its probability and sums the results.

discovery.text: Here: (0.5 × $200) + (0.5 × −$100) = $50. On average, you gain $50 per flip. It's a great bet.

twist.text: But expected value assumes you can play many times. A single bet that could ruin you is a different calculation.

climax.text: Expected value is the foundation of rational betting. It strips emotion and reveals the math underneath.

punchline.text: Multiply, sum, decide.

quiz.question: How is expected value calculated?
options: Multiply each outcome by its probability and sum

hook.text: A game offers infinite expected value. You still wouldn't pay more than $20 to play. Something is off.

buildup.text: In the St. Petersburg game, a coin is flipped until tails. Payoff doubles each round: $2, $4, $8, and so on.

discovery.text: The expected value is infinite—but no sane person pays a fortune to play because the big payoffs almost never hit.

twist.text: Daniel Bernoulli solved this in 1738 by introducing utility—the subjective value of money, not its face value.

climax.text: Your first million dollars transforms your life. Your billionth dollar barely registers. Utility is concave.

punchline.text: Infinite value on paper, finite value in life.

quiz.question: What did the St. Petersburg paradox reveal?
options: Money's subjective value (utility) matters more than face value

hook.text: A guaranteed $500 or a 50% chance of $1,200? Most people grab the sure money—even though the gamble pays more.

buildup.text: Risk aversion means preferring a certain outcome over a gamble with higher expected value.

discovery.text: It's rational when the downside could hurt you badly. Losing your rent money is worse than missing a bonus.

twist.text: Strangely, people become risk-seeking when facing guaranteed losses—they'll gamble to avoid a sure loss.

climax.text: Your risk tolerance should match the stakes. Small bets, expected value. Life savings, protect the downside.

punchline.text: Big upside means nothing if the downside ends the game.

quiz.question: When is risk aversion rational?
options: When the potential loss could cause severe harm

hook.text: People prefer a sure $1 million over a 10% chance of $5 million—but flip their logic in a nearly identical choice.

buildup.text: Maurice Allais showed people violate expected utility theory when certainty is involved.

discovery.text: We overweight certainty. A jump from 99% to 100% feels enormous; 50% to 51% barely registers.

twist.text: This means we don't process probabilities linearly—we warp them based on proximity to certainty.

climax.text: Prospect theory later formalized this: people use a distorted probability scale, not the real one.

punchline.text: Certainty warps probability like gravity warps light.

quiz.question: What does the Allais paradox demonstrate?
options: People overweight certainty and distort probabilities

hook.text: A gambler with a proven edge goes broke anyway. Why? He bet too much on each hand.

buildup.text: The Kelly criterion tells you how much to bet when you have a known edge—maximizing long-run growth.

discovery.text: The formula: bet the fraction equal to your edge divided by the odds. Edge of 10%, odds of 1:1, bet 10%.

twist.text: Betting more than Kelly grows wealth on average but dramatically increases the chance of ruin.

climax.text: Even with a guaranteed edge, bet sizing determines whether skill leads to wealth or bankruptcy.

punchline.text: Right bet, wrong size, still broke.

quiz.question: What does the Kelly criterion optimize?

hook.text: Flipping a coin is risky. You know the odds. Starting a business? Risky—but you don't even know all the risks.

buildup.text: Risk means known probabilities. Uncertainty means the probabilities themselves are unknown.

discovery.text: Frank Knight made this distinction in 1921. Most real-world decisions live in uncertainty, not neat risk.

twist.text: Standard expected-value math works for risk. For true uncertainty, you need different strategies entirely.

climax.text: Under uncertainty, diversify, stay flexible, and cap your maximum downside rather than chasing optimal outcomes.

punchline.text: Unknown odds need different rules.

quiz.question: What is the difference between risk and uncertainty?
options: Risk has known probabilities; uncertainty does not

hook.text: You packed an umbrella on a sunny day. Annoying—but imagine the regret of getting soaked without one.

buildup.text: Minimax regret: choose the option that minimizes your worst-case regret across all possible outcomes.

discovery.text: For each option, calculate: how bad would I feel if this turned out wrong? Pick the least-regrettable choice.

twist.text: It doesn't optimize for winning—it protects against the most painful what-if scenario.

climax.text: When you can't estimate probabilities, minimizing regret is a psychologically robust strategy.

punchline.text: Minimize the worst what-if.

quiz.question: What does the minimax regret strategy optimize?

hook.text: A new chemical seems safe—but long-term effects are unknown. Should you wait for proof of harm or proof of safety?

buildup.text: The precautionary principle: when potential harm is severe and irreversible, act cautiously even without full proof.

discovery.text: It shifts the burden of proof—instead of proving danger, we demand proof of safety before proceeding.

twist.text: Critics say it blocks innovation. Taken to extremes, nothing new would ever be approved.

climax.text: The key is proportionality: apply extra caution only when potential harms are catastrophic and irreversible.

punchline.text: When the stakes are permanent, caution is rational.

quiz.question: When does the precautionary principle apply?
options: When potential harm is severe and irreversible

hook.text: Before 2008, most financial models said a global banking collapse was virtually impossible. Then it happened.

buildup.text: Nassim Taleb coined Black Swan for rare, extreme events that standard models can't predict.

discovery.text: Black Swans have three properties: rarity, extreme impact, and retrospective predictability—we explain them after.

twist.text: Our models assume normal distributions. But real life has fat tails—extreme events happen far more than models expect.

climax.text: You can't predict Black Swans, but you can build systems that survive or even benefit from them.

punchline.text: Plan for the unplannable.

quiz.question: What defines a Black Swan event?
options: A rare event with extreme impact that seems predictable only in hindsight

hook.text: A friend turns down a stable job to freelance. Risky? Maybe—but freelancing keeps ten doors open instead of one.

buildup.text: Optionality is the value of having multiple future paths available without being locked into one.

discovery.text: Options have asymmetric payoffs: limited downside but potentially unlimited upside. That asymmetry is gold.

twist.text: Traditional planning picks one optimal path. Optionality-thinking keeps cheap options alive as long as possible.

climax.text: Under deep uncertainty, maximize the number of future choices rather than optimizing today's single best choice.

punchline.text: When lost, keep doors open.

quiz.question: What is optionality?
options: The value of keeping multiple future paths available

hook.text: Should you confess or stay silent? The answer changes depending on what your partner does. Welcome to strategy.

buildup.text: A payoff matrix maps every combination of your choices and your opponent's choices with resulting outcomes.

discovery.text: Reading the matrix reveals dominant strategies—moves that are best regardless of what the other side does.

twist.text: Sometimes no dominant strategy exists. Then your best move depends entirely on predicting the other player.

climax.text: Payoff matrices turn messy real-world conflicts into structured problems you can analyze logically.

punchline.text: Map the options. The strategy reveals itself.

quiz.question: What does a payoff matrix show?
options: Outcomes for every combination of players' choices

hook.text: Odysseus tied himself to the mast so the Sirens' song couldn't lure him overboard. He decided before temptation hit.

buildup.text: A commitment device is a choice you make now that restricts your future options to keep yourself on track.

discovery.text: Cutting off your own escape route sounds irrational—but it works because future-you can't be trusted with willpower.

twist.text: Hernán Cortés burned his ships in Mexico. His soldiers had no choice but to fight forward.

climax.text: Automatic savings, public commitments, and deadlines all work because they remove the future choice to quit.

punchline.text: Lock the door. Throw away the key.

quiz.question: What is a commitment device?
options: A way to keep all options open
A present choice that restricts future options to enforce follow-through

hook.text: The first company to dominate a market often keeps that lead for decades. But being first isn't always best.

buildup.text: First-mover advantage means acting early to grab resources, customers, or positions before competitors can.

discovery.text: Amazon, Google, and eBay all benefited massively from being early movers in their spaces.

twist.text: But MySpace, Friendster, and Netscape moved first too—and were crushed by patient second movers.

climax.text: First-mover wins when switching costs are high. Second-mover wins when learning from others' mistakes is cheap.

punchline.text: First or fast—know which game you're in.

quiz.question: When does first-mover advantage tend to succeed?
options: When switching costs are high for customers
When the product is easily copied

hook.text: A peacock's giant tail is useless for survival. That's the point—only a fit bird can afford the handicap.

buildup.text: Signaling means conveying hidden information through costly, hard-to-fake actions.

discovery.text: Michael Spence won a Nobel for showing how education works as a signal even if it teaches nothing practical.

twist.text: The signal must be costly to be credible. Cheap signals—like simply claiming you're great—convince nobody.

climax.text: Warranties, luxury brands, and engagement rings all work because they cost more than a liar would pay.

punchline.text: What you sacrifice says more than what you say.

quiz.question: Why must signals be costly to be credible?
options: Because expensive things are always better
Because cheap signals can be easily faked
Because cost is irrelevant to signaling

hook.text: You have to meet someone in New York with no way to communicate. Where do you go? Grand Central, noon—most people agree.

buildup.text: A Schelling point is a solution people converge on without communication, using shared cultural expectations.

discovery.text: Thomas Schelling showed that coordination depends on shared context, not just logic.

twist.text: There's nothing logically special about Grand Central. But its prominence makes it the obvious mutual guess.

climax.text: In negotiations, norms, and conflicts, Schelling points shape outcomes because people gravitate to the obvious.

punchline.text: The obvious answer wins when nobody can talk.

quiz.question: What is a Schelling point?
options: A solution people converge on through shared expectations

hook.text: At a county fair, hundreds guessed an ox's weight. The average guess was off by just one pound. The experts were worse.

buildup.text: The wisdom of crowds: large groups often estimate more accurately than individuals—even experts.

discovery.text: It works when guesses are independent, diverse, and decentralized. Each person adds a unique signal.

twist.text: When people copy each other—herding—the crowd becomes a mob and accuracy collapses.

climax.text: Prediction markets work on this principle: aggregate independent bets and the price reflects collective knowledge.

punchline.text: Many independent minds beat one brilliant one.

quiz.question: What condition makes the wisdom of crowds work?
options: Guesses are independent, diverse, and decentralized
The crowd must be very large

hook.text: Every advisor in the room agreed the Bay of Pigs invasion would succeed. Nobody dared disagree with Kennedy.

buildup.text: Groupthink occurs when a group prioritizes harmony and consensus over accurate analysis.

discovery.text: Irving Janis identified it after studying policy disasters—unanimous agreement despite obvious warning signs.

twist.text: The smarter and more cohesive the group, the more vulnerable it is. Trust breeds silence.

climax.text: Assign a devil's advocate. Invite outsiders. Reward dissent. Break the illusion of consensus.

punchline.text: Harmony killed the analysis.

quiz.question: What causes groupthink?

hook.text: Three friends rank pizza, sushi, and tacos differently. No voting system can always fairly combine their preferences.

buildup.text: Arrow's impossibility theorem proves no ranked voting system can satisfy all fairness criteria simultaneously.

discovery.text: Kenneth Arrow showed that with three or more options, every voting rule violates at least one reasonable fairness rule.

twist.text: This means all voting systems are imperfect—not broken, just inevitably compromised on some dimension.

climax.text: The question isn't which system is perfect. It's which tradeoffs matter most for your specific context.

punchline.text: Perfect fairness is mathematically impossible.

quiz.question: What does Arrow's impossibility theorem prove?
options: No ranked voting system satisfies all fairness criteria

hook.text: Each farmer adds one more sheep to shared land. Rational for each, devastating for all—the pasture collapses.

buildup.text: The tragedy of the commons: individuals acting in self-interest deplete a shared resource.

discovery.text: Garrett Hardin described it in 1968: oceans, air, groundwater—all shared, all vulnerable to overuse.

twist.text: Elinor Ostrom won a Nobel proving communities can manage commons without privatization—through local rules.

climax.text: The tragedy isn't inevitable. Trust, communication, and enforceable agreements can sustain shared resources.

punchline.text: Shared resources need shared rules.

quiz.question: What causes the tragedy of the commons?
options: Individuals depleting a shared resource through self-interest
Lack of resources to begin with

hook.text: Two kids fighting over cake? Let one cut, the other pick. Suddenly, both are incentivized to be fair.

buildup.text: Mechanism design is reverse game theory—designing rules so self-interested players produce good outcomes.

discovery.text: Instead of predicting behavior within a game, you design the game itself so the desired behavior is rational.

twist.text: Auctions, insurance deductibles, and tax brackets are all mechanisms designed to align incentives.

climax.text: The insight: don't fight self-interest—harness it. Make the right choice also the selfish choice.

punchline.text: Design the game so everyone wants to play fair.

quiz.question: What is mechanism design?
options: Designing rules so self-interested players produce good outcomes

hook.text: Judges grant parole 65% of the time in the morning but nearly 0% right before lunch. Hunger decided freedom.

buildup.text: Decision fatigue: the quality of your decisions deteriorates after making many choices in a row.

discovery.text: Your brain treats willpower and decision-making as a depletable resource—like a muscle that tires.

twist.text: This is why Steve Jobs wore the same outfit daily—he eliminated trivial decisions to save energy for important ones.

climax.text: Make important decisions early. Automate the trivial ones. Protect your mental bandwidth for what matters.

punchline.text: Fewer choices, better choices.

quiz.question: What causes decision fatigue?
options: Mental energy depleting after many decisions

hook.text: You're furious and about to send an angry email. Pause. How will you feel about this in 10 minutes? 10 months? 10 years?

buildup.text: The 10-10-10 rule forces you to evaluate a decision across three time horizons before acting.

discovery.text: Suzy Welch popularized this method to break the tyranny of present emotion over future wellbeing.

twist.text: Most regretted decisions optimize for the 10-minute feeling and ignore the 10-year consequence.

climax.text: The rule doesn't always change your answer—but it ensures you've considered all three time frames.

punchline.text: Zoom out before you zoom in.

quiz.question: What does the 10-10-10 rule help with?
options: Evaluating decisions across short, medium, and long time horizons

hook.text: Munger was asked how to live a great life. His answer: figure out how to guarantee a miserable one—then avoid that.

buildup.text: Inversion thinking asks: instead of how do I succeed, what would guarantee failure? Then avoid those things.

discovery.text: Jacobi, the mathematician, said it first: invert, always invert. Many hard problems become clear in reverse.

twist.text: It works because we're better at spotting obvious disasters than imagining ideal outcomes.

climax.text: Before any plan, list what would definitely make it fail. Remove those elements and what remains is stronger.

punchline.text: Avoid stupidity more than you seek brilliance.

quiz.question: What is inversion thinking?
options: Doing the opposite of what everyone else does
Identifying what guarantees failure, then avoiding it

hook.text: Your gut says invest. The spreadsheet says don't. Which one is right? Maybe both—they're answering different questions.

buildup.text: Two-track analysis runs intuition and analysis in parallel, then compares where they agree and diverge.

discovery.text: When both tracks agree, confidence rises. When they diverge, that's where the real thinking begins.

twist.text: Neither track is always right. Intuition misses data; analysis misses context and experience.

climax.text: Investigate the divergence. Your gut may have noticed something your spreadsheet can't model, or vice versa.

punchline.text: Disagreement between tracks is data.

quiz.question: What makes two-track analysis valuable?
options: It always chooses the intuitive answer
It compares intuition and analysis to find blind spots
It eliminates the need for data

hook.text: You agonized for weeks, chose perfectly—and the world changed the next day. Perfect planning met imperfect reality.

buildup.text: In complex systems, the feedback from a quick decision often teaches more than extended analysis could.

discovery.text: This is the explore-exploit tradeoff: sometimes acting fast and adjusting beats waiting for certainty.

twist.text: Perfectionism in decisions is itself a decision—to spend time instead of learning from action.

climax.text: Make fast, reversible decisions. Learn from the outcome. Adjust. Repeat. Speed beats precision in volatile environments.

punchline.text: Done, learned, adjusted beats perfect but late.

quiz.question: When is deciding quickly better than thorough analysis?
options: When decisions are reversible and environments are volatile
